exam: What key historical question differentiates FASD from a genetic syndrome? — Ask about quantity, frequency and timing of maternal alcohol intake during pregnancy.

A 3‑year‑old with growth below the 5th percentile, smooth philtrum and attention problems presents. Which diagnostic criteria do you apply first? — Use the revised Institute of Medicine criteria: facial features, growth restriction, CNS dysfunction.
How does ethanol‑induced oxidative stress affect fetal brain development? — Generates ROS that damage neuronal membranes and DNA, leading to apoptosis and impaired synaptogenesis.
Why is DNA methylation analysis not required for routine FASD diagnosis in low‑resource settings? — It is costly, not widely available, and clinical criteria are sufficiently sensitive.
In a setting without specialist dysmorphology services, what bedside tool helps identify FASD? — Use a standardized facial checklist (e.g., 4‑digit diagnostic code) and growth charts.
What preventive strategy would you prioritize in an antenatal clinic with limited staff? — Implement brief alcohol‑screening questionnaires followed by counseling at each visit.

A child with suspected FASD also has a heart murmur. Which condition should you consider and why? — Williams syndrome, because it presents with facial features and a characteristic supravalvular aortic stenosis murmur.
Explain why thiamine supplementation is not a primary treatment for FASD. — Thiamine addresses Wernicke’s encephalopathy, not the oxidative and epigenetic mechanisms of alcohol‑induced teratogenesis.
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Prenatal alcohol exposure disrupts fetal brain development through oxidative stress, altered neurotransmitter pathways and epigenetic changes. The syndrome presents with characteristic dysmorphic features, growth restriction and neurodevelopmental deficits. Understanding the biochemical mechanisms guides prevention and counseling in low‑resource settings.

b: Incidence higher where alcohol use is culturally accepted and prenatal care is limited.
Key triad: facial dysmorphism, growth retardation, central nervous system dysfunction.
sections.p: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) refers to a range of structural, neurocognitive and behavioural abnormalities caused by maternal alcohol consumption during pregnancy. It is the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide.

b: Oxidative stress damages neuronal membranes and DNA.
Ethanol alters retinoic acid signalling, crucial for craniofacial development.
Disruption of NMDA and GABA receptors impairs synaptogenesis.
sections.p: Ethanol crosses the placenta freely, reaching fetal blood concentrations equal to maternal levels. The fetus lacks mature alcohol dehydrogenase, so ethanol persists, generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) and interfering with cell signalling.

b: Global hypomethylation of neurodevelopmental genes.
Histone acetylation shifts that suppress neuronal differentiation.
sections.p: Normal embryogenesis depends on tightly regulated gene expression, epigenetic marks and growth factor gradients. Alcohol perturbs these processes through DNA methylation changes and histone modification, leading to lasting gene‑expression abnormalities.

b: Facial features: smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures.
Growth: intra‑uterine and post‑natal weight/height <10th percentile.
Neuro: microcephaly, intellectual disability, attention‑deficit, poor impulse control.
sections.p: The combined oxidative injury, disrupted signalling and epigenetic reprogramming produce the phenotypic features of FASD.

b: Screen pregnant women for alcohol use; brief counselling reduces risk.
Monitor growth charts and developmental milestones closely.
Coordinate with community health workers for early intervention.
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals, FASD may be under‑diagnosed because of limited access to genetic testing and reliance on clinical observation. Early recognition enables targeted neuro‑developmental support and prevents secondary complications such as malnutrition and school failure.

t.a: Detailed maternal history (quantity, timing of alcohol intake)
t.b: Establish exposure; if positive, raises suspicion for FASD.
Confirms growth restriction; <10th percentile supports diagnosis.

t.a: Facial photography or standardized dysmorphology checklist
t.b: Documents characteristic facial features; useful when specialist review unavailable.

b: Primary prevention: abstinence counseling, community education, integrate alcohol screening into antenatal visits.
Nutritional support: folic acid, vitamin B complex to counteract oxidative stress.
Early intervention: physiotherapy, speech therapy, special education programmes.
Behavioral therapy: address attention‑deficit and impulse‑control problems.
Monitor for secondary issues: growth failure, hearing loss, seizures.
sections.p: There is no cure; management focuses on prevention, supportive care and mitigation of neurodevelopmental deficits.

b: Down syndrome – flat facial profile, single palmar crease; genetic testing distinguishes.
Williams syndrome – ‘elfin’ facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis; cardiovascular exam key.
Congenital infections (TORCH) – microcephaly, intracranial calcifications; maternal infection history and serology help.
sections.p: Conditions sharing growth restriction and facial dysmorphism can mimic FASD.

b: Mild facial features can be subtle in older children; reliance on dysmorphology alone may miss cases.
Normal head circumference early in pregnancy does not exclude later microcephaly.
sections.p: Some findings may be absent despite significant disease.
